I’d probably say, “Look, there are jobs out there that need doing, and sometimes you just don’t have enough people willing or able to do them.” I’d see this especially in industries like agriculture, construction, or caregiving, where migrant workers often play a huge part in keeping things running. But I’d be cautious about how those roles are filled—I’d want to make sure that bringing in immigrants doesn’t drive down wages or make it harder for local workers to find good jobs. I’d ask, “Are we making sure these jobs pay a fair wage, so locals can compete too?”

When it comes to cultural diversity, I’d probably acknowledge its value but also want to emphasize balance. I’d say, “It’s great to have new ideas and traditions come into the mix, but it’s important not to lose sight of what holds us together as a country.” I’d want immigrants to embrace certain shared values, like respect for the law and a commitment to contributing to their communities. I’d feel that this helps keep the sense of belonging strong for everyone.

Security concerns are something I wouldn’t dismiss outright. I might say, “You can’t just ignore that some people are worried about crime or other risks. It’s not being unreasonable to want to feel safe.” That said, I’d also want real evidence to back up claims about rising crime rates or terrorism risks tied to immigration. I’d say, “Let’s look at the facts and not just go by fear or headlines. If there’s a problem, let’s fix it—but if there isn’t, let’s not make one up.”

The humanitarian perspective would resonate with me to an extent. I’d say, “I get it—there are people out there in the world dealing with things we can’t even imagine. If we can help some of them, that’s a good thing.” But I’d also be practical about it. I’d add, “We can’t help everyone—it’s just not possible. So we’ve got to make sure we’re taking care of the people here at home, too.” To me, there’d need to be a balance between compassion and practicality.

As for fears about employment and income, I’d think those are entirely reasonable concerns, especially for someone in the working class. I’d say, “If you’ve been working a job your whole life and suddenly you’re competing with someone who’s willing to do it for less, you’re gonna worry about that, and rightfully so.” I’d want policies in place that protect workers—both local and immigrant—from being exploited. I’d also want to see job training and education programs to help locals adapt to changing industries and job markets.

I’d probably feel that some perspectives, like the concerns about security or cultural integration, could use more dialogue and real evidence. I’d say, “Let’s talk these things out and see where the truth really lies.” But I’d also think that some issues, like employment concerns, don’t need much debate—they’re real and pressing, and they require action.

Overall, Character12_M would approach this with a mix of empathy and pragmatism. I’d want to make sure everyone’s voice is heard—whether they’re pro-immigration, concerned about its impacts, or somewhere in between. I’d probably sum it up by saying, “We’ve got to figure out a way to make immigration work for everyone—not just for the people coming in, but for the folks who’ve been here all along, too.”

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character12_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
J: As Character12_M, I’d say that none of these approaches on their own feels completely right. I’d probably lean toward some kind of middle ground that balances fairness with practicality and the needs of the community. Here’s how I’d break it down:

Complete openness—letting anyone come who wants to—might sound compassionate on the surface, but I’d find it unrealistic. I’d say, “Look, we’ve got limits on how much our schools, hospitals, and housing can take. If you open the floodgates, the system’s going to break, and then nobody wins—not the people already here, and not the people trying to come in either.” So that wouldn’t be an option I could support.

Refusing entry to workers from other countries entirely would feel too extreme in the other direction. I’d say, “There are jobs out there that need doing, and we don’t have enough people willing to do them. You can’t just slam the door shut and pretend those jobs don’t exist.” Plus, I’d think it would hurt industries that are important to the economy. That approach wouldn’t work either.

Now, admitting people based on job demand, that’s something I’d be open to. I’d say, “If there’s a genuine need for workers in certain areas, and we don’t have enough local folks to fill those roles, then it makes sense to bring people in to do the work.” But I’d want to make sure it’s done right. I’d push for rules that ensure jobs are offered to locals first and that anyone coming in gets paid a fair wage—not something that undercuts the people already working here. I’d also want to see strict enforcement of labor laws to prevent exploitation.

Setting numerical limits makes sense to me too because it recognizes that there are real limits to what our country can support. I’d say, “You’ve got to have a system with some checks and balances. Otherwise, how do you plan for things like housing, schools, or healthcare?” I’d want these limits to be flexible, though—adjustable based on things like job demands, the state of the economy, and humanitarian needs. It shouldn’t be a one-size-fits-all number, but it should be a number that reflects what’s realistic and sustainable.

The policy I’d favor would probably be a combination of admitting people based on job demand and setting numerical limits. I’d also want to make sure there’s a process to prioritize people in real need—like refugees fleeing war or persecution—because even though practicality is important, you can’t ignore the human side of things. I’d say, “If we’re going to offer people a chance to come here, let’s make sure they’re ready to contribute and that we’re ready to give them a fair shot at success. But let’s not bite off more than we can chew, either.”

To me, fairness means making sure that immigration doesn’t come at the expense of the people already here, while also recognizing the value and contributions that immigrants can bring to the table. I’d focus on policies that encourage social integration—things like language classes, job training programs, and community-building efforts—so that newcomers can really become part of the fabric of the country. I’d probably sum it up by saying, “We can be welcoming without being reckless, and we can be fair without turning our backs on the people who’ve been here all along. That’s the kind of balance we need.”

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character12_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*continuing as Character12_M*

Now, it's different - got the Vietnamese family on the corner, that young gay couple who moved in last year, the Muslim folks who I think are from Pakistan.

I don't have any problem with folks being different, long as they're good neighbors. That Vietnamese family - their boy helps me carry my groceries sometimes. Real respectful kid. And they keep their yard nice, better than some who've been here forever.

What matters to me is if people contribute, if they're trying to be part of things. I get frustrated with those who come here and then don't seem interested in becoming American, you know? I try to be friendly to everyone, wave and say hello. But I'll be honest - sometimes I feel a bit... uncomfortable, I guess, when I don't understand someone's customs or if they keep completely to themselves. Makes me wonder if they want to be part of our community at all.

Bottom line is, I judge folks by how they act, not where they're from. Are they decent? Do they look out for the neighborhood? Do they respect that there are ways we do things here? That's what matters to me when I'm sitting here watching everyone go about their day.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character12_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*continuing as Character12_M*

That's a tough one, especially for someone like me who's seen what happens when jobs dry up. When the plant downsized in '08, lots of good men I knew - guys with families, mortgages - they were out of work for months, some for years. Some never recovered.

In my view, fairness means taking care of your own first. I don't say that out of meanness, but it's like family - you make sure your kids are fed before inviting the neighborhood over for dinner. Americans who've paid into the system for decades, whose parents and grandparents built this country - they should get first consideration when jobs are scarce.

That said, I've worked alongside immigrants - legal ones - who were some of the hardest workers I've ever met. Fellow named Miguel at the plant, came here from Mexico legally in the '90s, man could outwork guys half his age. I respect that.

The balance I'd want to see is simple: legal immigration with limits that match what our economy can actually support. When times are good and we need workers, bring in folks who want to become Americans, who'll learn the language and follow our laws. But have the sense to slow it down when our own people are hurting.

What burns me is when companies bypass American workers because they can pay immigrants less or work them in bad conditions. That's not fair to anyone - exploits the immigrants and undercuts American wages. And illegal immigration? That's just jumping the line ahead of people doing it the right way.

I think we need better enforcement at the border, real penalties for businesses hiring illegal workers, and a streamlined system for legal immigration that prioritizes skills we actually need. And for those already here legally, they deserve the same protections as any American worker.

It's not about keeping people out because they're different - it's about having a system that's sustainable and doesn't leave our own citizens behind. A country that can't or won't take care of its own people first isn't much of a country at all, if you ask me.

My brother-in-law couldn't find American workers for his roofing business a few years back. So I understand that argument, especially for legal immigrants with skills we need.

The cultural diversity angle... *slight hesitation* I'm not against different cultures, but I do think we need a common American identity that binds us together. My grandparents came from Ireland, but they became American first and foremost. They learned English, adapted to the customs here. I worry when I see communities where that doesn't happen, where people stay isolated in their own cultural bubbles.

Security concerns - this needs honest talk without being called names. Most immigrants are decent folks, but it only takes a few bad actors. We should be able to discuss proper vetting without being called xenophobic. The government's first job is keeping citizens safe, so that's a legitimate concern in my book.

The humanitarian side... I'm a Christian man, and I believe in compassion. Genuine refugees fleeing persecution - we should help where we can. But there's a difference between refugees and economic migrants looking for better jobs. And we can't take in everyone from every poor country - there has to be limits based on what we can realistically handle.

As for impacts on jobs and wages - I've lived this. When a bunch of non-English speaking workers showed up at a construction site near me willing to work for half the going rate, local guys couldn't compete. That's just reality. Maybe economists can argue about the big picture, but I've seen the effects in my community.

What needs more evidence? I'd like honest numbers about costs - what immigrants contribute in taxes versus what services they use. No political spin from either side, just facts. And I'd like more research on assimilation - what helps immigrants integrate successfully and become part of American society.

What frustrates me is how this whole debate has become so black and white. Either you're for open borders or you hate immigrants. Most Americans like me are somewhere in the middle - we respect legal immigrants who contribute, but we want reasonable limits and expect people to become American in more than just paperwork. We can be both welcoming and have standards at the same time.

On the flip side, completely refusing entry to foreign workers doesn't make sense either. There are jobs Americans won't do or skills we're short on. My doctor is from India, and he's excellent - why would we want to keep someone like him out?

I'd favor a combination approach. First, we need secure borders - know who's coming in and have control over the process. Without that, nothing else matters.

Then, I'd prioritize based on skills and job demand - focus on bringing in people who fill actual needs in our economy. The tech industry, healthcare, specialized manufacturing - if we need those skills and Americans can't fill all the positions, let's bring in folks who can.

I'd definitely keep numerical limits, adjusted based on economic conditions. When unemployment is high here, we should reduce immigration accordingly. When we're at full employment and businesses are struggling to find workers, we can open the door wider.

For fairness, the system needs to be transparent and consistent. No special treatment based on what country you're from or who you know. Everyone follows the same rules, pays the same fees, meets the same requirements.

For social integration, I'd want requirements that immigrants:
- Learn English within a reasonable timeframe
- Take classes on American history and civics
- Demonstrate self-sufficiency through employment or having means to support themselves
- Pledge allegiance to America as their primary loyalty

I'd also support a probationary period before permanent residency, where immigrants show they're following our laws and integrating into society.

For refugees, I'd have a separate humanitarian quota - still with limits, but recognizing our moral obligation to help those truly fleeing persecution.

And for those already here illegally? That's tough. Mass deportation isn't practical, but blanket amnesty isn't fair to those who followed the rules. Maybe a middle path - come forward, pay a penalty, get background checked, and get in line behind those doing it legally.

This kind of balanced approach would maintain America as a nation of immigrants while ensuring we remain one nation, not a collection of separate groups. It recognizes both our humanitarian values and the practical limits of what our country can absorb. Most importantly, it puts the interests of American citizens first while still being welcoming to those who want to come here the right way and truly become American.

responses.answer:
Well… if I’m being him for a minute, like he’s sitting right here with his coffee in that old chipped mug he always used—then yeah, fairness to Character12_M wasn’t about everybody getting the same thing. That should count for something.”  

Fairness, to him, meant you don’t get handed everything, but you shouldn’t be kicked while you’re trying to climb. He saw too many guys like him—guys from the shop floor, the loading dock, the ones who wore their work boots home covered in grease—watch jobs disappear or get undercut. And when folks came in from somewhere else and seemed to get help he never got? That stung. Not because he didn’t want people to make it, but because he’d ask, “Where was that help for me when I was sleeping in my car during the layoff in ’09?”

Sense of belonging… that one cut deep. He grew up in a neighborhood that felt like *his*—same faces, same churches, same diners where they knew your order. Over the years, he saw it change. Not always bad—but fast. And sometimes without anyone asking the people already there how they felt about it. He didn’t hate difference—he served with Black and Latino guys in the Navy, respected them more than most politicians—but he believed belonging went both ways. You come here, you learn the language, you respect how things run. Don’t expect us to bend over backwards for you while our own kids can’t afford rent.

Community, to him, wasn’t just living near each other. It was looking out for one another. It was knowing who’s sick, who lost a job, who needs a ride. He worried that when people don’t share a common language, a common understanding of law or duty or even just how to treat a neighbor, that web starts to fray. He wasn’t against helping refugees or folks down on their luck—but he’d say, “Let’s make sure we’re not breaking the back of the folks who’ve been here, paying taxes, raising families, and getting ignored.”

One time—he told me this story once at the VFW—he was helping organize a winter coat drive. They had donations piling up, but then the city brought in a group of newly resettled families, no notice, 30 people dropped into the low-income housing behind the strip mall. Nobody from the community was consulted. No volunteers briefed. And suddenly, there were tensions—noise, trash, some break-ins. Not everyone, mind you. But enough. And he said, “We wanted to help. But we weren’t included. It made it harder to care. Like our own town didn’t matter anymore.”

So to him, fairness meant earning your place without being cheated. Belonging meant mutual respect—not just tolerance. And community? That was earned slowly, by showing up, by doing right by your neighbors. And he believed immigration could fit into that—but only if it didn’t leave the working stiff, the guy who stayed through the hard times, feeling like an outsider in his own hometown.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character12_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*[Sits back slightly, eyes scanning the garden like he’s really seeing it—the raised beds, the broken fence line, the mix of faces]*

You know… I’ve been coming to this garden since it was just a patch of dirt behind the old rec center. Used to be mostly folks like me—retired tradesmen, widows on fixed incomes, a few young moms trying to grow something fresh for their kids. We’d swap seeds, tools, sometimes a six-pack and a bench story or two. Simple.

Now? Well… it’s different. Got folks here from halfway across the world. Some from places I couldn’t even point to on a map before. You see Somalis in their long dresses tending peppers like they’ve done it for generations—turns out, they have. Got a Vietnamese family three plots over growing herbs I’ve never seen, but damn if it don’t smell good. And there’s a young gay couple—white, local-born—from down the street, who show up every Saturday with compost and jokes. Hell, even got a guy who used to live under the bridge until the outreach program found him housing—he shows up now, quiet, keeps to himself, but he weeds better than most.

Do I mind the variety? Not really. People work the soil, they usually mean well. There’s honesty in that.

But… it ain’t always smooth. Like when Mr. Hassan didn’t understand why we rotate crops—damaged the whole south bed because he planted the same thing twice. Took weeks to fix. Or when the new refugees didn’t know about water restrictions and flooded the walkways. No malice—just didn’t know. But then old man Peterson yells at them in English they barely grasp, and it turns ugly fast.

And yeah, some neighbors… they struggle. Real struggle. I see the woman on Elm who drinks all day on her porch, kids running around barefoot. I see the meth pipe hidden near Plot 7 last month. Doesn’t matter what race or where they’re from—pain looks the same. But when it’s layered on top of language gaps, or different ideas about property, or how loud is too loud at midnight—that’s when the cracks show.

I’ll tell you this—I try to nod, say “Morning,” offer a spare tomato. I learned enough Spanish in the Navy to get by. I don’t fear these people. But I won’t lie and say I feel *connected* to most of them. We don’t share stories. Don’t go to the same churches. Don’t remember the same things—like when the factory closed, or how the river flooded in ’98. That shared memory? That’s what built this town. And now it feels like we’re all living side by side, but not together.

So do I want them gone? No. But I want us to meet in the middle. Learn our ways. Respect the rules we lived by. Not come in and act like none of it matters—or worse, like we’re the ones who need fixing.

Belonging isn’t automatic. It’s earned. And it goes both ways.

So when I see that couple holding hands at the garden, I don’t glare. I mind my business. If they keep their plot clean, say hello, respect others’ space? Then fine. We coexist.

But here’s where tolerance needs work—on both sides.

See, I’ve watched Somali women cover head to toe, praying in the shade by Plot 12. Respect that. But then one day, they refused to shake my hand—said their faith forbade it. Okay. Their belief. But then their boys yell at Mrs. Kowalski for wearing shorts in her garden like she’s immoral? That ain’t respect. That’s disrespect under the cover of religion.

Same with language. If you’re on public aid, living in housing I helped pay for through taxes, then you oughta speak enough English to read a street sign, fill a prescription, or understand “no trespassing.” Don’t expect me to learn Somali so you can ignore the country’s language.

And family structure? I was raised—man and woman, married, kids—worked for me. But I see these young couples now, living together five years, no ring, bouncing from apartment to apartment, maybe a kid or two along the way. Feels unstable. Like nobody’s accountable. And when things go south? The kid suffers. Not judging—but stability matters. Especially for children.

So what makes everyone feel comfortable?

Simple: mutual effort.

You want me to accept your differences? Then show me you’re trying to be part of this place—not just parked here waiting for a check. Show up. Learn the rules. Keep your space clean. Speak the language well enough to function. Don’t demand special treatment because of your background.

And us old-timers? We gotta quit acting like the world owes us a museum exhibit. Times change. Can’t freeze everything in 1975. If new folks work hard, raise decent kids, don’t cause trouble? Then they earn their place—same as anyone.

But let’s not pretend all choices are equal. Some ways of living lead to stronger communities. Others—like chronic drinking, untreated illness, raising kids in chaos—hurt the whole block. And we should be allowed to say that without being called hateful.

Tolerance isn’t blind acceptance. It’s living together *despite* differences—because we agree on the basics: respect, decency, responsibility. Lose those, and the garden doesn’t grow. No matter how many cultures we claim to celebrate.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character12_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*[Sighs, rubs his knee like it aches—old injury from the shipyard—and looks down at the dirt under his boots]*

Fairness? When jobs are thin and folks back home are hurting? Fairness means *first things first.*

I’ll say it plain: if there’s a job open, and there’s three guys who’ve lived here 30 years, paid taxes, raised families, maybe even lost work when the plant downsized—and then we bring in workers from another country to fill that same job? That ain’t fair. Not one bit.

Now don’t get me wrong—I’m not against immigrants working. Never have been. I worked alongside Puerto Ricans in Norfolk, Mexicans in Texas shipyards. Good people. Hard workers. But they came legally, learned English, didn’t expect handouts. And most importantly? They weren’t brought in *because* American workers were turned away.

But now? It feels backwards. You see ads for “H-2B visa jobs” in the paper—landscaping, meatpacking, chicken plants—places where guys from my union used to work. Jobs that pay lousy but still feed a family. And they’re giving them to foreigners—*on visas*, so the boss can pay less, fire ‘em easy, no benefits. Meanwhile, my buddy Ray—he’s 58, two bad knees, but strong hands—can’t get called back at the warehouse because “they prefer the new hires.” Why? Because they’re cheaper. Disposable.

That ain’t competition. That’s rigging the game.

So how do I balance it?

Simple: *locals first.* If there’s an American citizen—doesn’t matter his race, doesn’t matter where he was born on this soil—who’s willing, able, and qualified to do the work, he gets first shot. No exceptions. And if the employer says, “Well, nobody applied,” then prove it. Make ‘em post the job locally, offer training, hire from within the community before they go begging for foreign labor.

And let’s talk about public resources while we’re at it. When hospitals stay open late treating undocumented patients with no insurance—that cost hits us. Schools translating notices into seven languages, hiring extra staff—paid for by property taxes *I* pay every month. Food stamps, housing vouchers, Medicaid—when those are stretched thin, and I see families born here waiting months for assistance while newcomers get fast-tracked through nonprofit programs funded by grants nobody told *us* about? That breeds resentment. Not because we’re heartless—but because it feels like the rules changed without our say.

I served my country. I showed up. I played by the book. So did millions like me. We didn’t ask for much—just a chance to work, keep our homes, retire with dignity. Now it feels like that loyalty’s being punished while others jump the line.

So balance isn’t equal access. Balance is *priority.* Prioritize the people who built this place. Who defended it. Who paid into it.

Let migrants come—if there’s room. If they’re filling jobs nobody else *can* do, not just jobs Americans won’t do because they’re underpaid or mistreated. Fix the wages, fix the conditions, then see if locals won’t take ‘em.

And for God’s sake, enforce the damn borders. Not because I hate anyone—but because an open door with no control kills fairness. It turns community into a free-for-all.

You want to help refugees? Fine. Do it overseas. Resettle them through order, not overflow. Bring them in numbers we can absorb—without breaking schools, hospitals, housing.

Because when times are tight, fairness means remembering who’s already here. The quiet ones. The ones who never complained. The ones still showing up, day after day, hoping the system hasn’t forgotten them.

We’re not asking for special treatment. Just not to be last in line.

That part needs more honesty. Not more slogans.

**“Cultural diversity brings vitality.”**  
I’ll give you this: food’s better now. You can get a damn good taco or halal chicken wrap on Main Street. And festivals? The Diwali thing last fall—the lights, the music—was nice. Real nice. Didn’t hurt anybody.

But “vitality” doesn’t feed my grandkid. Doesn’t fix potholes. And when people say, “Diversity is our strength,” like it’s gospel? Feels like they’re talking over folks like me. Like my culture—blue-collar, church-going, flag-waving—is something to be ashamed of. Like if I say, “I miss how things used to be,” I’m suddenly a bigot.

No. I lived through change. I adapted. But don’t tell me my way of life has no value just because it ain’t flashy.

**Security concerns—crime, tensions, terrorism.**  
Now here’s where I get quiet. Because I don’t like saying it out loud—but I think about it.

I know most immigrants aren’t criminals. Most are running *from* crime. But then I read about MS-13 dumping bodies in Long Island. Or a guy on a terror watch list getting asylum. Or the meth coming across the border with cartels tied to it. And I think: *we’re not checking hard enough.*

And crime isn’t just felonies. It’s showing up at the ER with tuberculosis and nobody knowing their history. It’s kids in school who don’t speak English, acting out, teachers overwhelmed. It’s Section 8 housing packed with families three deep while veterans sleep in trailers. That’s not crime—*but it feels like disorder.* And disorder makes people scared. Makes them pull in.

Are immigrants more violent than natives? Don’t know. Maybe the stats say no. But I’ll tell you what I *see*: when communities change fast, without planning, without integration, tensions rise. You got guys from rural Guatemala walking into neighborhoods where people lock their doors at night—and neither side knows how to talk to each other. Of course there’s friction.

We need real dialogue—not politicians telling us “diversity is strength” while the local library gets vandalized and nobody explains why.

**Humanitarian reasons—refugees, poor regions.**  
Look… I served. I saw starving kids in the Philippines. Saw war zones. So no—I don’t have a heart of stone. If someone’s fleeing bullets, torture, death? Yeah, we should help. We’re supposed to be better than that.

But how many? How fast? And where does it stop?

We took in refugees after Vietnam, after Kosovo. Good. But those were limited, vetted, resettled with support. Now it feels like the floodgates are open and nobody’s asking, “Can we handle this?” Schools full. ERs backed up. Shelters overflowing. And again—where’s the priority for *our* poor? My niece waited nine months for Section 8. Meanwhile, new arrivals get housing, cash, phones—because grants cover it. Is that fair?

Helping others is noble—until it breaks the people already here trying to hold on.

**Fears about jobs and income?**  
Those fears aren’t myths. They’re real. I’ve been in union halls when the news came: “Contract went to migrant crew—lower bid.” Why? Because they’re paid less. No health insurance. No pension. Bosses love it. Wall Street loves it. But working folks? We feel it in our wallets.

And it’s not just manual labor. I’ve got a nephew trying to get into construction—can’t get apprenticeship. “Too many H-2Bs,” they say. Meanwhile, wages stay flat. Benefits vanish. That’s not conspiracy—that’s what I see with my own eyes.

So which views are reasonable?

All of ‘em—*partly.*

People who say immigrants work hard? True.  
People who say they strain systems? Also true.  
People who fear crime? Some fear is exaggerated—but not all.  
People who preach compassion? Good impulse. But compassion without limits becomes self-destruction.

What needs more evidence?  
The *numbers.* Not headlines. Not activist claims. Not Fox News panic. I want to see:  
- How many jobs are really going unfilled *after* fair outreach to locals?  
- What’s the actual fiscal impact—taxes paid vs. services used—by different immigrant groups?  
- How thorough is vetting for security risks? Can we trust it?  
- How fast are communities changing compared to integration rates?

And dialogue? Hell yes we need it. But not staged town halls with smiling faces and photo ops. I mean real talks—workers, neighbors, cops, pastors—sitting down, saying: *“This is what I see. This is what I fear. This is what I hope.”* Without being called racist for speaking plain.

Because the truth is—we’re all trying to survive. Immigrants included. But fairness means remembering that the guy born here, staying put, paying taxes for 40 years? His voice matters too.

And right now? He feels like he’s shouting into the wind.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character12_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*[Takes off his cap, runs a hand through thinning gray hair, then puts it back on slow—like he’s weighing each word before it leaves his mouth]*

Complete openness? No. That’s not policy—that’s surrender. You can’t just say “come on in” and expect a working town, a school system, a hospital, to handle it without breaking. I love this country, but it ain’t infinite. We got limits. And when you ignore them, the people who pay are the ones already struggling—the renters, the underpaid, the ones with no safety net.

Refusing *all* foreign workers? No, that’s dumb too. I’ve seen crops rot in fields because nobody was there to pick ‘em. Factories shut down waiting on welders. Some jobs need filling—and if we can’t train or hire fast enough, then fine, bring someone in. But on *our* terms.

So what do I want?

A mix. Tight, fair, and controlled.

**First: numerical limits.** Yeah. Set a number—based on what our economy *actually* needs and our communities can absorb. Not what lobbyists want. Not what charities push. Not what politicians use for votes. A real, honest cap. And stick to it. Like a fishing quota—you don’t drain the lake.

And within that number? Priorities.

**One: family reunification—but only immediate.** Spouse, minor kids. That’s it. I get it—people want their folks together. But I’ve seen chain migration where one cousin gets in, then brings five more, then those five claim ten more. Boom—in two years, a whole new neighborhood that speaks one language and owes nothing to the place they’re living in. Enough. Keep families together, sure. But don’t turn America into an endless sponsorship game.

**Two: humanitarian cases—refugees, asylum—yes, but vetted.** Properly. Not rushed. I’m not scared of poor people—but I am scared of being played. If someone’s fleeing war or tyranny, fine. Let ‘em in. But check their names. Know their history. Don’t take 100,000 a year if we can’t house, teach, or employ them. Do it smart. Do it slow. Compassion without order isn’t kindness—it’s chaos.

**Three: job-based immigration—tied to real labor gaps.** Not wants. *Gaps.* And prove it. Employer says, “I can’t find anyone”? Then show me the job was advertised locally. Show me union was consulted. Show me wages are at market rate—or higher. No undercutting American workers.

And here’s the thing—**temporary doesn’t mean permanent.** H-2 visas? Fine. But if the guy’s here for a season, he goes *home* after. No backdoor path to citizenship because “he worked hard.” He knew the deal. We’re not running a guestworker-to-citizen pipeline unless *we* decide to open that door—with debate, not default.

And while we’re at it—**require integration.** Language. Civics. Not optional. If you want to stay beyond temporary status, you learn English. You know the laws. You understand how things work here—not just how they worked back home. That ain’t cruel. That’s how you become part of us.

No free rides either. Use public services? Pay taxes first. No welfare the day you arrive. Earn it.

Now—balance fairness and social integration?

Fairness means the guy who’s been here 40 years, paid dues, lost his job in the recession—he matters too. His concerns aren’t “hate.” They’re *grievances.* And if we keep ignoring them, resentment grows. Not just toward immigrants—but toward the whole system.

Integration fails when we treat newcomers like guests and locals like ghosts.

So my policy?  
- **Limited numbers.**  
- **Real labor needs.**  
- **Full vetting.**  
- **No unchecked chain migration.**  
- **Temporary means temporary.**  
- **English and civics required.**  
- **Local workers first—always.**

And enforce the damn border. Not with cruelty—but with control. Because when people cross illegally, it insults everyone who waited, applied, followed rules. It tells the honest ones: “You were a sucker for trying.”

I don’t hate immigrants. But I love my neighbors more. The ones who stayed. Who showed up. Who still believe in this place—even when it feels like it’s forgetting them.

A good policy wouldn’t make me choose between compassion and country.  
It would make sure both could survive—together.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character12_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character12_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*[Pauses a long time. Takes off his glasses, wipes them slowly on his shirt—like he’s not quite ready to speak yet]*

You know… I thought I knew him well. We fished together. Drank cheap beer on his porch. Talked politics, sure—but usually in broad strokes. “Country’s changing too fast,” he’d say. “Don’t feel like mine no more.” Stuff like that.

But sitting here today, really trying to *be* him—not just remember him—I saw something deeper.

I always figured his views came from bitterness. Age. Fear of change. Maybe a little racism tucked in there somewhere. I didn’t say it out loud—but I thought it. Like a lot of us do. We hear older white guys complain about immigrants, and we assume the worst.

But stepping into his shoes like this… I felt the weight he carried. Not hatred—but *loss.* A life spent working, obeying rules, paying taxes, raising kids right—and watching the rewards fade. Watching jobs vanish. Watching neighborhoods shift without being asked. Watching people come in who don’t speak the language, don’t follow the customs, get help he never got… and being told, “Be grateful. They’re hard workers.”

That cuts deep when you’ve *been* a hard worker.

I realized—he wasn’t against immigration because he hated difference. He was afraid of being erased. Of becoming irrelevant in a place he helped build. That ain’t bigotry. It’s grief.

And that made me rethink my own stance.

I’ve always leaned open-door. Compassion first. Global outlook. But I live in the city. Got education. Work online. Immigration doesn’t threaten my job. My world adapts easy.

He lived in a town where every change felt like a threat. Where one factory closing could wreck a generation. Where schools scrambling to translate everything meant less attention for *all* the kids—including his grandkids.

So today… I see now: it’s not just about what’s legal or humanitarian. It’s about *belonging.* And belonging has to go both ways. You can’t demand loyalty to a community while making its longtime members feel like strangers.

That doesn’t mean close the gates. But it means slow down. Plan better. Protect the middle and working class—*native-born and newcomer alike.* Pay fair wages so jobs don’t depend on exploitation. Invest in integration—language, training, civic duty—so people become neighbors, not just residents.

And listen—to people like him. Not to shout them down. Not to label them. But to hear the hurt beneath the grumbling.

Because Character12_M? He loved this country. Deeply. Not perfectly. Not blindly. But with the love of someone who gave his years to it. And when love feels unreturned… it turns quiet. Withdrawn.

Today reminded me—he wasn’t wrong to want fairness.  
He was just tired of being last.

And if I’m honest?  
This conversation didn’t just bring him back.  
It made me a little more willing to listen—to folks I used to dismiss.  
And that… that’s something he would’ve appreciated.
